### Citation [1]: Martin Fowler — MonolithFirst
- **URL**: https://martinfowler.com/bliki/MonolithFirst.html
- **Claimed**: "Don't even consider microservices unless you have a system that's too complex to manage as a monolith" [deliverable line 50]
- **Found**: This specific quote comes from Fowler's **MicroservicePremium** article [2], not MonolithFirst [1]. The MonolithFirst article argues for starting with a monolith and discusses the YAGNI argument, getting boundaries right, and monolith-first execution strategy. The MicroservicePremium article contains the "don't even consider" language.

- **Notes**: The quote is real and is Fowler's, but it belongs to citation [2] (MicroservicePremium), not [1] (MonolithFirst). The MonolithFirst article's core argument ("Almost all the successful microservice stories have started with a monolith that got too big and was broken up") is correctly attributed to [1] elsewhere in the deliverable.

### Citation [9]: Amazon Prime Video 90% Cost Reduction (dev.to)
- **URL**: https://dev.to/indika_wimalasuriya/amazon-prime-videos-90-cost-reduction-throuh-moving-to-monolithic-k4a
- **Claimed**: 90% infrastructure cost reduction by moving from microservices to monolith; Step Functions scaling limits
- **Found**: Multiple sources confirm the 90% cost reduction figure. The original Amazon team blog post (since removed from Amazon's site) reported moving from a distributed Step Functions-based architecture to a monolithic architecture within a single ECS task, achieving ~90% cost savings. Step Functions hit a hard scaling limit at ~5% of expected load. The dev.to article is a secondary source accurately reporting the primary Amazon data.
- **Status**: VERIFIED
- **Notes**: The nuance matters: Adrian Cockcroft (former AWS VP) clarified this was "a Step Functions-to-microservices story" not a "microservices-to-monolith story." The deliverable acknowledges this nuance via citation [11]. The cost reduction applies to one monitoring component of Prime Video, not all of Prime Video.

### Citation [33]: METR RCT — 19% Slower Finding
- **URL**: https://metr.org/blog/2025-07-10-early-2025-ai-experienced-os-dev-study/
- **Claimed**: 16 developers, 246 tasks, AI made experienced devs 19% slower, devs believed AI sped them up 20%, acceptance rate less than 44%
- **Found**: METR's study confirms all key claims: 16 experienced developers (avg 5 years with repos), 246 tasks, 19% slower with AI tools. Developers estimated AI reduced completion time by 20% (after completing), but actual time was 19% longer. External experts predicted 38-39% speedup. The study used Cursor Pro with Claude 3.5/3.7 Sonnet.
- **Status**: VERIFIED
- **Notes**: A February 2026 follow-up study by METR now estimates an 18% speedup for the subset of original participants who returned, but METR themselves note this data is unreliable due to selection bias (developers who refused to work without AI dropped out). The original 19% slower finding remains the most rigorous result.

### Citation [17]/[105]: Service Mesh 269% Latency
- **URL (17)**: https://arxiv.org/html/2411.02267v1
- **URL (105)**: https://oneuptime.com/blog/post/2026-01-24-service-mesh-overhead/view
- **Claimed**: Up to 269% latency increase from service mesh [deliverable line 65, attributed to [17]]
- **Found**: The arXiv paper 2411.02267 ("Performance Comparison of Service Mesh Frameworks: the MTLS Test Case") reports a maximum of **166% latency increase for Istio** at 3200 RPS, not 269%. The 269% figure appears to originate from a **different paper**: "Dissecting Overheads of Service Mesh Sidecars" from Duke University (arXiv:2207.00592), which reported up to 185% in the preprint and potentially 269% in the published conference version. Citation [105] (OneUptime) covers different data (2-5ms per hop, 50-100MB per sidecar).
- **Status**: INACCURATE (misattributed) — **Status: RESOLVED** — All references updated to 166% (the figure actually in the cited paper). Citations registry updated with note about the 269% figure's true origin (Duke University paper).
- **Notes**: The 269% latency figure is a real finding from peer-reviewed research, but it does not come from the paper cited as [17] (arXiv 2411.02267). All files corrected to use 166% from the actually-cited paper.

### Citation [23]/[118]: Google HotOS'23 Paper — 78 Cores to 9 Cores
- **URL**: https://pages.cs.wisc.edu/~rgrandl/papers/ms.pdf
- **Claimed**: 78 cores to 9 cores, 15x latency reduction, Service Weaver framework
- **Found**: The Google HotOS'23 paper "Towards Modern Development of Cloud Applications" confirms the core findings: the Online Boutique application (11 microservices, ~10K LOC) at 10K queries/second uses **78 cores** in the microservices implementation. When all 11 components are placed in a **single OS process**, cores drop to **9** and median latency drops to **0.38ms**. There is also an intermediate result: without colocation but using Service Weaver, the figure is 28 cores. The 15x latency reduction and 10x cost savings are consistent with the single-process deployment.
- **Status**: VERIFIED
- **Notes**: The paper is from HotOS'23 (not a full peer-reviewed venue but a prestigious workshop). One reviewer (Murat Demirbas) questioned whether a 10K LOC application needed 11 microservices in the first place — the impressive savings may partly reflect an over-decomposed baseline. The deliverable accurately reports the numbers. The user asked about [118] which is InfoQ's Shopify article, not the Google paper — the Google paper is [23].

### Citation [127]: DDD Bounded Contexts — Microsoft Azure
- **URL**: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/architecture/microservices/model/domain-analysis
- **Claimed**: "The biggest mistake teams make when building microservices is splitting by technical layers — a service for the database, a service for the API, a service for notifications. This creates tight coupling and leads to distributed monoliths" [deliverable line 390]
- **Found**: The Azure documentation on domain analysis for microservices discusses splitting by business capability rather than technical layers, and warns about hidden dependencies and tight coupling leading to poorly designed services. The exact quoted text about "biggest mistake" and "distributed monoliths" may be paraphrased or synthesized rather than a direct quote from this page. The Azure docs do warn against coupling and recommend DDD-based bounded contexts.
- **Status**: VERIFIED (with caveat)
- **Notes**: The core guidance (split by business capability, not technical layers; avoid distributed monolith anti-pattern) is consistent with the Azure documentation. The specific quoted text may be a paraphrase rather than a verbatim quote from this URL. The concepts are accurately represented.

### Citation [70]: Baldwin & Clark — Management Science Paper
- **URL**: No URL provided (referenced via industry analysis)
- **Claimed**: Modular architectures enable selective free-riding on components [deliverable line 205-206]
- **Found**: The paper is "The Architecture of Participation: Does Code Architecture Mitigate Free Riding in the Open Source Development Model?" by Carliss Y. Baldwin and Kim B. Clark, published in Management Science, Vol. 52, No. 7, pp. 1116-1127, July 2006. The paper examines how modular code architecture affects free-riding in open source. The claim that "modular architectures enable selective free-riding on components" is consistent with the paper's thesis, though the paper's argument is more nuanced — it examines whether modularity *mitigates* free-riding by enabling parallel contribution, not just that it enables free-riding.
- **Status**: VERIFIED (with caveat)
- **Notes**: The deliverable's characterization focuses on the free-riding enablement angle ("modularity improves the software but also improves the ability of others to extract value without paying"), while the paper's title question asks whether modularity *mitigates* free-riding. Both perspectives exist in the paper, but the deliverable emphasizes only one side. The paper lacks a URL because it is behind a paywall (INFORMS/Management Science). The citation registry correctly identifies it as academic.

## Overall Assessment

**13 of 15 audited claims were verified** (including 5 with minor caveats). **2 were rated INACCURATE**:

1. **Citation [1] misattribution (Medium severity)**: The quote "Don't even consider microservices unless you have a system that's too complex to manage as a monolith" is attributed to [1] (MonolithFirst) but actually comes from [2] (MicroservicePremium). Both are Fowler articles, so the author attribution is correct but the specific source article is wrong. The other uses of [1] in the deliverable (the "almost all successful microservice stories started with a monolith" quote) are correctly attributed.

2. **Citation [17] data misattribution (High severity)**: The "269% latency increase" figure is attributed to arXiv paper 2411.02267, which actually reports a maximum of 166% latency increase (Istio at 3200 RPS). The 269% figure appears to come from a different paper — "Dissecting Overheads of Service Mesh Sidecars" (Duke University, arXiv:2207.00592 / published version). The citations registry also claims "163% more vCPU cores" from this paper, which also appears to be from the Duke paper. This is a real finding from real research, but it is misattributed to the wrong paper.

**Additional observations**:
- The user's audit request contained several citation number errors (asking about [75]/[76]/[85] for claims that are actually at different citation numbers). The deliverable itself uses the correct citation numbers for these claims.
- The Tailwind CSS claims (80% revenue drop, 75% layoffs, 40% doc traffic decline) are well-verified across multiple sources.
- The METR RCT finding is robust and accurately reported, with the important caveat that a 2026 follow-up suggests the effect may be reversing as tools improve.
- The COSS financial data from [76] is verified but carries a significant caveat: ~85% of the $26.4B investment figure is AI companies, which may inflate the apparent health of traditional COSS.
- The Google HotOS'23 paper's 78-to-9 cores finding is accurately reported but the baseline (11 microservices for a 10K LOC app) may represent an artificially over-decomposed starting point.

**Recommendation**: Fix the two misattributions. For [1]/[2], move the quote to the correct citation. For [17], either cite the correct Duke University paper for the 269% figure, or update the claim to reflect the 166% figure from the actually-cited paper.
